newsitem.title: USA: New York City may get extra windfall - NYS official.
newsitem.headline: New York City may get extra windfall - NYS official.

text.p: The New York State Deputy Comptroller for New York City on Thursday said that much like New York State, the city might see a late surge in tax revenues giving it another windfall in the 1997 fiscal year.

Noting the city's revenues already were running ahead of estimates by as much as $600 million, Rosemary Scanlon told Reuters Financial Television in an interview, "We see the possibility of another $50 million to $100 million before the end of the year."
The interview will be shown Thursday at 1515 EST.

Scanlon also praised New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani for not inflating his estimates of how much Wall Street banks and brokerages, whose strong earnings produced most of the windfalls reaped by the city and state, will earn in the 1998 fiscal year, which for New York City begins on July 1.

"I would grant him the credit of having a rather moderate forecast outlook on his revenues for the next fiscal year," she said, though she cautioned the volatile nature of the financial sector's earnings is a concern.

The city said that Wall Street firms, which earned an estimated $11.5 billion last year, will only earn around $4.7 billion next year. In part due to this industry's profits, New York State looks for its 1997 surplus to exceed its initial $1.3 billion estimate.

And Scanlon identified another big risk facing the city: the challenge of finding jobs for people now on welfare. "Clearly, at the moment the greatest uncertainities are on the economic end because the workfare requirements under the new (federal) welfare bill suggest that people must come off welfare and go to work after two years," she said.
The city already has a high unemployment rate, and the new rules could mean 80,000 new job seekers will be competing for positions.
